title: AegisGrid POC budgeting + latency runway scoping
summary: Kickoff scoping for a 6-week POC focused on unit economics and latency runway. Goals: define success criteria, collect sample traffic for benchmark, estimate per-token costs under varying batching/caching profiles, schedule a 72-hour benchmark. Action items: Redwood to send cost model & benchmark plan; customer to share logs and confirm budget ceiling.
action_items: Jordan Park: send detailed cost model spreadsheet and hosted vs dedicated delta by 2027-06-25
Maya Singh: draft benchmark plan (models, input distribution, AMI/container list) by 2027-06-29
Rita Chen (AegisGrid): provide 7 days of traffic logs + canonical prompt set by 2027-06-24
Sophie Reed: confirm max monthly budget and procurement timeline by 2027-06-28
next_steps: Redwood to run initial token-econ calc and share heatmap
Customer to provide test account + access for on-prem sim (if requested)
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-06-22
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Rita Chen (CTO, AegisGrid), Marco Alvarez (ML Engineer), Sophie Reed (Head of Platform)

Auto-summary: kickoff for POC focused on cost/perf tradeoffs. Discussed target latency SLOs (90th percentile), throughput targets, batching strategies (dynamic batching), prefix/KV cache opportunities, and benchmarks to run. Action items captured.

[00:00:00] Jordan Park: hey everyone, uh thanks for joining, i'll kick us off. i'll be jordan, i'm the AE on this account, and maya will do the technical run through. can folks briefly intro?
[00:00:12] Rita Chen: hey, i'm rita, cto at aegisgrid. we run an energy trading platform, low-latency alerts, and a lot of short prompts for classification and streaming explanations.
[00:00:22] Marco Alvarez: marco here, ml eng, i'll be owning the POC on our side. mainly interested in throughput and the cost runway.
[00:00:28] Sophie Reed: sophie, platform. i'll coordinate infra and procurement.
[00:00:33] Maya Singh: hi all, maya from redwood, i work on SE, latency and batching are my jam. excited to dig in.

[00:01:00] Jordan Park: quick agenda: success criteria, workload sizing, what benchmarks look like, timeline, and then next steps. start with success criteria — rita, what does success look like for you at the end of the POC?
[00:01:15] Rita Chen: good question. two buckets: first, performance — we need 95th percentile latency under 300ms for our short inference path (avg prompt ~80 tokens). second, economics — we need to demonstrate a cost per inference under $0.003 at our projected scale, and show predictability for monthly budgeting. third, security — we need VPC deployment with KMS integration for keys.
[00:01:40] Jordan Park: good, so lat and unit cost + security. maya, any quick thoughts on feasibility?
[00:01:47] Maya Singh: yeah, superficially those are achievable. couple of clarifying q's: 1) what's your expected qps? 2) what's typical prompt/response length distribution? and 3) how tolerant are you of occasional tail latency spikes if we can lower median cost?
[00:02:05] Marco Alvarez: target average qps is 250 sustained during trading hours, with bursts to 1k for flash events. prompt distribution: 70% are under 100 tokens in, outputs are ~60 tokens on average, some longer explainers up to 400 tokens but that's <5% of traffic. on tail latency: we really care about 95th in the short path, those explainers can be async.
[00:02:30] Maya Singh: perfect. that helps. with 250qps and that token mix we should look at batching windows of 10-30ms to keep latency tight but still get batching gains. caching: sounds like a lot of repeated prefixes — any templated prompts?
[00:02:45] Rita Chen: yes, many prompts reuse the same instrument ids and templated language, so prefix caching could help.

[00:03:10] Jordan Park: on the econ side, high level — we usually model per-token cost based on model selection, quantization, and batching. for hosted vs dedicated, the delta often comes from reserved GPU amortization and faster kernels. maya, can you sketch a sample per-token ballpark for a 7B-style open model vs a 13B quantized?
[00:03:28] Maya Singh: sure. rough numbers, ballpark: hosted 7B quantized with good batching: $0.0009 per 1k tokens (so $0.0000009 per token?) [laughs], let me rephrase: about $0.0009 per token per 1k — sorry, transcription glitch — actual: $0.0009 per 1k tokens means $0.0000009 per token, yeah. 13B quantized on hosted maybe 2-3x that. on dedicated with reserved capacity and kernel tuning we often see 30-50% reduction in per-token when you amortize costs at scale, especially if you can use int8 kernels. but exact depends on sequence lengths and KV cache hit rates.
[00:04:05] Marco Alvarez: that decimal's tripping me up. can you give an example: my average request is 140 tokens total (in + out). what's our per-request cost on hosted 7B vs dedicated 13B with caching?
[00:04:18] Maya Singh: sure, for 140 tokens: hosted 7B cost ~= 140 * 0.0000009 = 0.000126 USD per request. for 13B hosted maybe ~0.00035 per request. dedicated 13B with good quantization and caching maybe 0.00018 per request. again these are estimates; we will run bench to nail numbers.
[00:04:40] Rita Chen: our finance folks want monthly run rate for 250 qps sustained. can we quickly compute that?
[00:04:48] Jordan Park: 250 qps sustained is ~21.6M requests per day? actually 250 * 3600 * 24 = 21,600,000. times the per-request cost is big. maya, can you do quick per-month $ calc?
[00:05:02] Maya Singh: monthly requests ~648M (21.6M * 30). with hosted 7B at $0.000126 per req that's ~81,648 USD per month. hosted 13B would be ~227k. dedicated 13B (0.00018) would be ~116.6k. these are rough, and batching/caching can drive numbers down — e.g., if prefix KV cache reduces avg tokens processed by 25% effective or batching increases throughput w/o proportional token cost, numbers shift materially.
[00:05:36] Sophie Reed: ok that's in the ballpark. our max monthly budget for a pilot is $120k. so dedicated 13B might just fit if we can hit the assumed caching gains.
[00:05:45] Marco Alvarez: what about dynamic batching — will that push tail latency above 300ms?
[00:05:52] Maya Singh: depends on batch windows and qps distribution. with 250qps sustained, 10-15ms batching windows can yield sizable throughput without adding more than ~10-20ms to p99 for short requests. the larger risk is burst to 1kqps — we need autoscale headroom and fallback model variants. we can set policy to prefer latency SLO, falling back to a smaller model when capacity constrained.
[00:06:15] Rita Chen: fallback to smaller model — do you see semantic regressions? we can't have incorrect trading signals.
[00:06:21] Maya Singh: yes regressions possible; part of the POC is a quality regression test set. we can measure semantic drift and set thresholds. often for short classification tasks, smaller models perform similarly; for nuanced explainers we keep the larger model and route them to async.

[00:06:45] Jordan Park: security and deployment: rita mentioned VPC + KMS. we support private deployments with customer-managed VPC peering and KMS integration, as well as an on-prem package if needed. any constraints?
[00:06:58] Sophie Reed: procurement will push for a private plane with SSO, audit logs, and SOC2 attestation. are audit logs per token available?
[00:07:08] Maya Singh: we emit structured audit logs and we can capture request metadata (route, model, duration). we don't log raw user data unless configured; for the POC we can enable full request logging to your secure bucket. KMS/HSM integration is available for keys.

[00:07:30] Marco Alvarez: benchmark plan — what will you run?
[00:07:33] Maya Singh: propose a 72-hour run simulating your production distribution: 70% short (<=100 tokens), 25% mid (100-400), 5% long (>400). we'll run on hosted and dedicated variants, varying batching windows (10ms, 25ms, 50ms), and enable prefix caching toggles. we'll capture latency percentiles, throughput, GPU utilization, and per-token cost by model. we'll also instrument KV cache hit rate to quantify savings.
[00:08:00] Rita Chen: and what do you need from us to run that?
[00:08:04] Maya Singh: sample traffic logs, canonical prompts, and a test account or secure endpoint to push traffic. ideally a small dataset of 5k–10k representative prompts. also indicate any IP ranges or VPC endpoints if we need to hit a private deployment.

[00:08:20] Jordan Park: timeline — we propose: customer shares artifacts by 6/24, redwood shares cost model + benchmark plan by 6/25–6/29, schedule benchmark week of 6/28, run 72-hr test and deliver results + recommendation within one week after run. is that feasible?
[00:08:36] Sophie Reed: procurement timeline may slide but we can prioritize sample artifacts. i'll confirm budget and PO process by monday.

[00:09:00] Marco Alvarez: two technical nitpicks: 1) will batching reduce token-level accuracy due to attention truncation or kvcache issues? 2) how do you measure effective tokens billed vs raw tokens — are you charging on input+output or only generated tokens?
[00:09:18] Maya Singh: good questions. 1) batching does not change model semantics; it only groups in-flight requests. attention truncation is controlled by max seq lengths; we'll use streaming for long outputs to avoid truncation. kv cache is per-session; when we use prefix caching we can reuse cached keys to avoid recomputing. 2) billing is token-usage-based and for hosted we show input + generated tokens in billing. our cost model will break down input vs output and show where caching reduces effective token processing.

[00:09:50] Rita Chen: what about quantization artifacts? we've seen hallucinations increase a bit with aggressive int4 on some tasks.
[00:09:57] Maya Singh: right — quantization is a knob. for classification/short tasks int8 or int4 often is fine but for nuanced generation we recommend int8 or bf16. in the POC we'll include quality baselines per quantization level so you can pick the acceptable tradeoff.

[00:10:20] Jordan Park: any competitors or existing stack we should be aware of?
[00:10:24] Rita Chen: we did a small eval with openai endpoints plus a test on aws sagemaker endpoints. finance asked about self-hosting via replicate for cheapest per-token but ops complexity was high.

[00:10:40] Maya Singh: noted. we'll include a competitor delta slide in the output.

[00:11:00] [long-ish silence as folks review numbers]
[00:11:20] Marco Alvarez: ok, lessnoise: what are the likely failure modes in the benchmark? e.g., cold-start for kv cache, model OOMs, autoscale lag. which do you expect and mitigations?
[00:11:32] Maya Singh: exactly those. cold-starts reduce cache hit rate early in run; we'll seed cache with common prefixes to simulate steady-state. OOMs we catch by choosing appropriate batch size and activation memory; dedicated nodes let us pick bigger VM sizes. autoscale lag — we'll provision a modest buffer and use fast spin-up images. we'll also run a canary ramp to exercise scaling.

[00:12:00] Rita Chen: seeding cache — can you show us how much benefit we should assume?
[00:12:05] Maya Singh: typically prefix caching hit rates can yield 15–40% token reductions for templated workloads. for your stated templating i expect mid-20s. we'll measure during the POC.

[00:12:30] Jordan Park: tough Q from finance: can you provide a 12-month run-rate forecast for 250qps with 20% caching and a 30% batching uplift?
[00:12:40] Maya Singh: to produce a credible 12-month forecast we need some assumptions on growth and reserved commitments. but quick calc: baseline monthly spend hosted 7B ~81.6k (from earlier). with 20% caching that drops to ~65.3k. with batching gains we can drop effective per-token cost further maybe 15–25% leading to ~49–55k. if you commit to dedicated reserved capacity, cost becomes more stable and you'd be in the ~40–60k band depending on amortization and utilization. we'll put a modeled spreadsheet with scenarios.

[00:13:20] Sophie Reed: that helps. procurement will want to see a contract tier that includes an SLA for 95th latency and a negotiated overage rate.
[00:13:29] Jordan Park: we can provide SLA-backed dedicated offerings and adjust overage terms. i'll include legal in followups.

[00:13:45] Rita Chen: on benchmarks — you mentioned measuring GPU utilization. do you provide the raw perf traces? we need to feed those to our infra team.
[00:13:53] Maya Singh: yes, we'll share raw traces, flamegraphs, kernel logs, and a summary report. plus a CSV with per-minute token counts, p50/p95/p99 latency, and cost breakdowns per model/quantization.

[00:14:10] Marco Alvarez: minor ask — can we run an initial micro-benchmark on our side with a smoke test? maybe 1k qps for an hour to validate request shapes before the full 72-hr?
[00:14:19] Maya Singh: absolutely, we recommend a smoke ramp. we can provide a load generator script and a sample harness.

[00:14:30] [discussion about who does procurement steps]
[00:14:50] Jordan Park: quick recap & next steps: 1) aegisgrid to send sample logs + prompts by 6/24 (Rita/Marco). 2) redwood to send cost model spreadsheet by 6/25 (Jordan) and detailed benchmark plan by 6/29 (Maya). 3) schedule the 72-hr benchmark week of 6/28 (all). 4) sophie to confirm budget and procurement timeline by 6/28. 5) run micro smoke test once test account is provisioned.
[00:15:20] Rita Chen: sounds good. one last thing — can we get an estimate for data egress costs if we choose hosted?
[00:15:27] Maya Singh: yes, we'll add egress and storage costs to the spreadsheet; for most inference workloads egress is small relative to token processing but if you stream many long outputs it matters.

[00:15:40] Sophie Reed: thanks all. any open questions?
[00:15:44] Marco Alvarez: none from me.
[00:15:46] Jordan Park: great — we'll follow up with the docs mentioned. thanks everyone.

[00:15:55] End of recording

Notes on transcription quality: speaker labels occasionally overlap; some numeric decimals transcribed confusingly; proper nouns (e.g., KV cache, VPC) sometimes appear as K-V or VPI.
